draft.title: Tone and its effect
card: Tone is the attitude a writer shows toward the issue and the reader. It comes through word choice, sentence length and the way the writer addresses opponents.
Outraged
angry and urgent, with strong words and short, sharp sentences. It can stir readers to share the anger, but it may seem extreme to some.
Measured
calm and fair, with careful words and a reasonable voice. It can make the writer seem balanced and trustworthy.
Sarcastic
mocking, saying one thing and meaning the opposite. It can make an opposing view look silly, but it may put off readers who agree with that view.
draft.remember: Tone is the writer's attitude, and it shapes how readers feel about the issue and the writer.

a.q: A writer calls a council plan "a brilliant idea, if you enjoy sitting in traffic". What is the tone?
opts: Sarcastic, mocking the plan by saying the opposite
Measured, giving a fair and calm view of the plan
Outraged, showing urgent anger at the council
Measured, praising the plan with careful words
a.why: The writer says brilliant but means the plan is bad, which is sarcasm. It is not outraged, because the words are mocking rather than angry and urgent. It is not measured, because it makes the plan look silly instead of weighing it fairly.
a.clue: Does the writer mean what the praise says?

b.q: Priya writes about a proposed ban on phones in schools. She says some students may lose a useful tool, but argues the ban would still help most classrooms. What effect does her tone most likely have on readers?
opts: It makes her seem fair, so readers may trust her
It makes readers feel angry at the people who disagree
It makes her opponents look foolish to readers
It makes readers feel she is shocked and desperate
b.why: Admitting a point against her view and using calm words is a measured tone. This can make her seem balanced and trustworthy. Anger or mockery would come from outraged or sarcastic tones, which her words do not show.
b.clue: Look at how calmly she treats the other side.

a.best: Sarcastic, mocking the plan by saying the opposite

b.best: It makes her seem fair, so readers may trust her

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with a hedge ('readers may trust her'). The distractors all say flatly 'It makes...', so a test-wise student could pick it without knowing the idea.
